## The idea

Choose degrees 1, 3, and 5 of a major scale and you have its tonic triad. Begin
on degree 2 and choose every other degree again; another chord appears without
introducing a pitch from outside the key. Continue from all seven starting
points and the scale itself determines a family of triads. Their different
qualities emerge from its unequal spacing.

These are *diatonic chords*. Roman numerals name their scale position and encode
quality: uppercase for major, lowercase for minor, with a diminished marker on
degree 7. A progression such as `I, V, vi, IV` therefore stores relationships
instead of fixed note names. Bind it to another key and every pitch changes,
while the sequence of harmonic jobs stays recognisable.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :piano

define :diatonic_triads do |root|
  notes = scale(root, :major).to_a
  7.times.map do |degree|
    [notes[degree], notes[(degree + 2) % 7], notes[(degree + 4) % 7]].
      each_with_index.map { |pitch, i| pitch + (i > 0 && pitch < notes[degree] ? 12 : 0) }
  end
end

define :render_progression do |root, numerals|
  lookup = {I: 0, ii: 1, iii: 2, IV: 3, V: 4, vi: 5, vii_dim: 6}
  chords = diatonic_triads(root)
  numerals.each do |numeral|
    play_chord chords[lookup[numeral]], release: 1.6
    sleep 2
  end
end

progression = [:I, :V, :vi, :IV]
[:c3, :d3, :e3, :f3].each do |key|
  puts "key #{key}"
  render_progression key, progression
end
```

The four passes climb through different keys while tracing the same harmonic
route. I establishes home; V raises the expectation of return; vi diverts that
expectation toward a related minor chord; IV opens another path back toward I.
Because one symbolic array drives every rendering, the common behaviour is
easier to hear than it would be in four unrelated note lists.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the progression with `[:I, :IV, :V, :I]`. Hear how V now spends its
   tension on an immediate tonic rather than on a diversion to vi. The final
   boundary should close more firmly.
2. Print the seven C-major triads as MIDI integers and compare the sizes of their
   two thirds. The resulting pattern is major, minor, minor, major, major, minor,
   diminished; it is derived rather than stored in the code.
3. Arpeggiate each chord in the renderer. The progression and pitch content stay
   fixed, while separate attacks reveal which alternating scale degrees make
   each harmony.

## Why it works

The scale array contains seven distinct degrees and a repeated octave. To build
a triad, select every other degree. Modular indexing wraps the upper selections
to the beginning of the seven-note collection; octave correction then restores
their ascending order above the current chord root.

No quality table is needed. The spacing already present in the major scale
produces the familiar major-minor-minor-major-major-minor-diminished pattern.
Roman-numeral symbols become keys into that generated chord array. Score data
can then say what progression is intended, while the renderer decides which
concrete notes express it in the current key.

Case carries information that a bare integer degree would lose. `:V` states both
position and the major quality expected in a major key. Later, a chromatic chord
may alter that default, and an explicit symbolic layer gives the alteration a
place to be represented. Reducing everything to zero-based indices too early
would erase the distinction the notation is trying to communicate.

Roman numerals also make comparison across keys practical. The dominant of C
major and the dominant of F major contain different pitch classes, but both
occupy the same formal position and direct energy toward their own tonic. This
is late binding in a musical form: the progression stores intent, and
`render_progression` resolves it against a root. A collection of MIDI arrays can
be transposed, but it does not explain why one chord follows another.

The lookup exposes the limits of the short symbol. Major `:I` and minor `:i`
need distinct defaults, while inversion is better stored as another field than
encoded in a proliferation of names. A fuller record could hold `:degree`,
`:quality`, and `:bass`, leaving concrete voicing to the renderer. For this
diatonic comparison, the compact symbols work because their defaults are clear.

## Take it further

Write `progression_notes(root, numerals)` so it returns chord arrays without
playing them. Evaluate `[:vi, :IV, :I, :V]` in all twelve roots. Each result
should contain four three-note chords, and every pitch class should belong to
the corresponding major key. Once those structural checks pass, choose one key
and render it with inversions selected using Lesson 27's `voice_near` idea. The
same symbolic plan should survive both validation and voicing.
